title: LLM API Differentiation Playbook - GTM Micro-Scripts and Technical Rebuttals
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact, operational playbook for AE/SDR/SEs to use when engaging teams currently evaluating LLM API providers. Focus is on pragmatic differentiation vs general-purpose LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex, Cohere, Hugging Face). It emphasizes engineering-first objections (latency, determinism, cost), procurement questions (SLA, data controls), and micro-scripts tailored to persona.

Positioning thesis (one-liner):
Redwood is the inference platform that treats serving as the product — predictable latency, predictable cost, and predictable security across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Key value pillars (quick elevator bullets):
- Predictable performance: SLA-backed latency across predictable capacity tiers and Dedicated pools.
- Cost control: batching/kv-cache/quantization recommendations + tooling to quantify token economics.
- Deployment parity: same API and controls across hosted, dedicated, and VPC/private modes.
- Reliability & fallbacks: model variant routing and automated graceful degradation to protect user experience.

Persona-specific battle snippets:
1) Product/ML engineer (care about output quality, latency, iteration speed)
- Pain they voice: "We need consistent tail latency for real-time features and to avoid cost spikes."
- Micro-script: "You can start on hosted API and mirror the same API contract to Dedicated when throughput or isolation matters — same SDK, same eval hooks. We’ll run a head-to-head on your prompt set to show median + p95 latency and token-cost delta across a 24h workload snapshot."
- Technical evidence to offer: per-route p50/p95 traces, sample KV-cache hit rates, sample quantized model latency stats, short reproducible notebook.

2) Platform / Infra (care about ops, throughput, SREs)
- Pain: "We need autoscaling without noisy neighbor effects and a predictable budget."
- Micro-script: "Dedicated pools provide reserved capacity and predictable queueing characteristics; autoscaling policies are configurable and we offer traceable routing rules so you can cap burst spend.
We also provide deployment policies to fallback to smaller, cheaper variants when capacity is constrained."
- Evidence: example autoscale policy configs, capacity planning spreadsheet, SLO playbook.

3) Security / Compliance / Legal
- Pain: "Can you guarantee data residency and encryption keys?"
- Micro-script: "Private deployment gives you the control plane in your VPC with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; we can support an air-gapped on-prem bundle for highly regulated workloads."
- Evidence: compliance checklist, SOC2 report stub, sample contract language for data residency.

Competitor shorthand (how to frame without going into vendor trash):
- OpenAI / Anthropic: excellent base models + dev velocity. Weak spots: limited private deployment, pricing unpredictable at scale, limited routing controls.
- Google Vertex: deep platform integrations but often heavier on price and not built for dedicated inference economics; control plane lock-in risk.
- Hugging Face / Cohere: flexible model access; customers often have to assemble their own serving/inference stack to get low latency and unit costs.

Feature comparison script (for quick AE prep)
- Ask first: "Is what you care about model access or serving economics?" This frames the conversation.
- If model access: acknowledge and pivot to ops: "Great — you can bring models, but how are you planning to serve them with predictable latency and cost?"
- If serving economics: lead with Redwood Optimize and Dedicated options.

Traps and neutralization (common red flags customers get from competitors and how to respond)
- "We can replicate your features ourselves."
  Response: "You could, but maintaining predictable tail-latency and cost across traffic spikes requires a non-trivial ops investment (kernel selection, dynamic batching, KV cache correctness). We provide audits and example TCO calcs showing typical infra and SRE hours saved over 12 months."
- "They offer model X cheaper per token."
  Response: "Per-token is only one axis — you should look at per-inference cost factoring in latency SLOs, necessary instance types, and engineering time to manage fallbacks and rollouts. We’ll size a cost-comparison using your sample traffic shape."
- "Switching vendors is hard."
  Response: "We emphasize API parity and a migration kit. For Dedicated/Private customers we offer an onboarding plan with runbook handoffs and a short-term dual-run period to make change low-friction."

Deep technical rebuttals (for SEs)
- Latency objections: provide p50/p95 numbers on same GPU class, show how quantization and kernel selection reduce latency, and provide trace with KV cache on/off. Explain why batching can be tuned to maintain tail SLOs.
- Model quality tradeoffs: show examples of evaluations where a slightly smaller model + prompt engineering + temperature controls gives 90% of quality at 40% of cost. Offer to run the customer's eval set.
- Data residency: explain Private deployment topology (control plane in customer VPC, optional air-gapped inference nodes) and certificate/KMS flows.

Scripts and short templates (copy/paste friendly)
- Discovery email (prospect):
  "Hi <Name>, saw you’re evaluating LLM providers. Quick note — we help teams cut per-inference cost and lower p95 latency without rewriting inference code. Can we run a 48-hour bench on a 1k prompt sample and show concrete per-route delta?"
- Slack/LinkedIn connect (compact):
  "Curious how you’re handling inference economics at scale — we help teams move from model experiments to production-grade serving (predictable latency/SLA + VPC/private deploy)."

Quantification playbook (how to make value tangible)
- Step 1: Get a 24–72h sample of production traffic or a 1k prompt set with distribution characteristics (seq lengths, real-time vs batch).
- Step 2: Run Redwood bench vs candidate provider on identical GPU families and public model variants. Collect p50/p95, token cost, and throughput.
- Step 3: Build a 12-month TCO that includes committed capacity, SRE headcount estimate, and fallback overhead. Present delta as projected monthly savings and latency improvements.

Objection flows (common dialog trees)
- "We already have a relationship with X": acknowledge, ask what keeps them up at night, offer a non-invasive bench.
- "Pricing is the main blocker": ask for target unit economics and offer to show a tailored Optimize plan that usually reduces token spend 10–40% without changing models.

Operational enablement items for reps to attach to outreach
- 1-page latency vs cost cheat sheet (per-model, per-GPU family)
- Onboarding checklist for Dedicated/Private
- 2-slide customer ROI snapshot template (fill in from bench)

Open questions / items to pull from Product & Bench team:
- We need a canned 1k-prompt bench script that runs on demand and outputs a standard JSON with p50/p95, tokens, and KV-cache hit rate. (Owner: bench team)
- Standard legal language for MSA around data residency and KMS keys (Owner: Legal)

Next steps (for AE/SE workflows)
- Use this note as the single source for micro-scripts until the broader battlecard library is updated.
- For any prospect where latency or cost is a top-2 decision factor, trigger a bench run and involve Solutions Eng in the first week.
- Capture the bench outputs into the ROI snapshot and include it in the next exec touch.

Notes / informal:
- Keep tone neutral and engineer-first; avoid vendor-bashing.
- This doc is intentionally concise — expand with new competitor intelligence as we gather more loss reasons.
